summary: Defines an address allocation policy that encodes the address of the Rendezvous Point (RP) inside an IPv6 multicast group address. For PIM Sparse Mode, this works as a group-to-RP mapping mechanism and simplifies multicast configuration across domains.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3956 defines IPv6 multicast addresses that carry the address of their rendezvous point. PIM-SM routers can read that address from the group address instead of relying on a separate group-to-RP mapping.

questions: how does embedded rp work in ipv6 multicast
what is the riid field in an ipv6 multicast address
subtitle: How an IPv6 multicast group address can identify its PIM rendezvous point.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Any Source Multicast lacked the inter-domain source-discovery mechanism used with IPv4, while Source-Specific Multicast did not cover every need described by the RFC.
tldr.mechanism: Embedded-RP marks a unicast-prefix-based IPv6 multicast address and places the rendezvous point's network prefix and interface identifier in that address. PIM Sparse Mode routers derive the RP from the group address.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism can simplify RP discovery without per-domain Bootstrap Router configuration. RFC 3956 updates RFC 3306 and is itself updated by RFC 7371.

today: RFC 3956 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3306 and is updated by RFC 7371. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Multicast Mapping Problem
sections.content:
In Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), a Rendezvous Point (RP) coordinates multicast sources and receivers for a group. IPv6 had no Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) mechanism to share active-source information across domains. Source-Specific Multicast avoids that problem, but the RFC says it was not expected to be the only inter-domain solution in the short term.

This document defines an address allocation policy that encodes the RP in an IPv6 multicast group address. It calls these embedded-RP addresses and defines how PIM-SM maps the group to its RP. The method also applies to scoped intra-domain Any Source Multicast and can be used for automatic RP discovery in situations that otherwise use the Bootstrap Router protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The group address itself can identify the RP for that group. Routers use the address to find the RP instead of learning the mapping separately.

sections.title: The Embedded-RP Address Format
sections.content:
The format builds on the unicast-prefix-based multicast address in RFC 3306. This RFC assigns the R flag and uses four bits for the RP Interface ID (RIID), while keeping the prefix length, network prefix and group ID fields. The flag sequence is shown as 0RPT.

When R is 1, P and T must also be 1, producing the prefix FF70::/12. When R is 0, the older address meaning applies and RIID must be zero. The behavior of some other flag combinations is unspecified; implementations should not treat FFF0::/12 as Embedded-RP without a further IETF specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A flag marks an address as one that contains an RP address. The address also reserves a small field for the RP interface identifier.

sections.title: Deriving and Checking the RP Address
sections.content:
An address qualifies for this mechanism only if it is in FF70::/12, its prefix length is not zero, and the prefix length is no greater than 64. The first rule excludes Source-Specific Multicast addresses; the second prevents the prefix from overlapping the group ID.

To derive the RP, a router copies the first plen bits of the network prefix into a zeroed 128-bit IPv6 address, then replaces the last four bits with RIID. RIID zero is reserved. Routers must apply the usual RP-address validity checks to the result and exclude at least fe80::/10, ::/16 and ff00::/8, because the encoded value comes from an untrusted source.
sections.plainLanguage: A router copies the stated network-prefix bits into an empty IPv6 address and adds the RIID at the end. It checks that the result is a permitted RP address before using it.

sections.title: Address Allocation Examples
sections.content:
The examples use the network prefix 2001:DB8::/32. An administrator can place an RP on a subnet and use a more specific prefix, or use the /32 prefix and set an RP address such as 2001:DB8::y. In the latter arrangement, the address can be assigned as a loopback address and injected into routing.

The RFC also shows a customer multicast prefix whose embedded RP remains 2001:DB8::y, because plen specifies how many prefix bits form the RP, not necessarily the length of the multicast allocation. These examples demonstrate choices for assigning group identifiers while keeping the RP mapping tied to the selected network prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that an operator can choose a broad or specific network prefix for the RP. The group allocation can be more specific while the same prefix bits still identify the RP.

sections.title: Operating and Controlling RPs
sections.content:
The address-to-RP binding makes some failover approaches harder to use unchanged. The RFC discusses PIM-based Anycast RP and advertising a shared RP address in the interior routing system, but leaves redundancy mechanisms outside its scope. An RP can use an IPv6 unicast prefix up to /64, with the interface identifier configured to match RIID; RIID zero must not be used.

Because the group address specifies its RP, the PIM domain does not need BSR or another RP mapping protocol for these groups. Operators still need to control which groups an RP serves. The RFC notes that filtering advertisements alone does not stop outsiders from joining a group; PIM scoping at borders is an example of stronger protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators must plan RP placement and redundancy because the group address points to a particular RP. They can also limit which multicast groups an RP accepts.

sections.title: PIM-SM Operation and Scale
sections.content:
PIM-SM uses the derived RP for reverse-path lookups, Join/Prune processing and Register encapsulation. For FF70::/12 addresses, Embedded-RP mapping must take priority over other mapping methods to avoid loops and inconsistencies. Routers may cache derived mappings, but the mapping may need to be calculated for each group address.

When a receiver joins, its router sends a PIM-SM Join toward the RP encoded in the group address. A sender's router sends Register messages carrying the packets toward that RP. The RFC's model removes inter-domain MSDP information distribution, while noting that the RP-centered arrangement changes where source traffic travels and that RP failure handling needs care.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver's router reads the RP from the group address and sends the normal PIM-SM Join toward it. The address changes the mapping step, while the remaining PIM-SM message flow stays in use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the RP address is visible in group addresses, it can be easier to identify and may be exposed to attack. RPs must handle Join, Prune and Register messages from Designated Routers, creating possible denial-of-service pressure. The RFC recommends that a router act as an RP only when explicitly configured and says an RP can filter the groups it serves.

Routers must validate the derived RP address as they would an address learned by another method. Operators can also configure allowed multicast prefixes. The RFC warns that hiding group information is not a substitute for real protection; it points to boundary scoping as one option.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoded RP can be found by anyone who sees the group address. Operators should secure RP routers, check derived addresses and control which groups an RP serves.

viz.caption: FIELDS IN THE MODIFIED IPV6 MULTICAST ADDRESS

fields.name: Multicast marker
fields.desc: The leading IPv6 multicast address bits.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The 0RPT flag bits identify Embedded-RP when R, P and T are set.

fields.name: RIID
fields.desc: RP interface identifier copied into the derived RP address.

fields.name: Prefix length
fields.desc: Number of network-prefix bits used for the RP.

fields.name: Network prefix
fields.desc: Prefix bits from which the RP address is derived.
